\title{The pathwidth complex}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
The minimization of open stacks problem (MOSP) asks for the order in which to
make a set of patterns so that the fewest customer orders are open at once.
\citet{LY2002} listed twelve problems from operations research, VLSI design and
graph theory, MOSP among them, as equal to it ``plus or minus one'', and gave
no proofs. We ask which of these equalities are true, and what follows when
results, algorithms and benchmarks are moved between the twelve problems
through pathwidth, the quantity that connects them. We find four things. First,
eight of the twelve rows are exact, counting pathwidth itself: each equals
pathwidth or pathwidth plus one. Two lie in bands one and two wide, and two are
false as stated; every relation is proved, and machine-checked in Lean.
Second, the literature has settled on the name pathwidth, used more than three
times as often as the other eleven names together, and the three communities
rarely cite one another. Third, the best exact algorithm for MOSP, the search of
\citet{ChuStuckey2009}, is a pathwidth algorithm, and two of its published
dominance theorems are false. The correct rule was already known for
pathwidth; we show that it is tested by one bipartite matching per candidate,
and prove the repaired search sound. In our implementation it costs at most
2\% more search nodes on each benchmark set, and it re-proved all 115 benchmark
optima that rested on the published rules, changing none. Fourth, we release
17,714 benchmark graphs, distinct up to isomorphism, from twenty collections,
16,087 of them with a certified pathwidth and a layout that attains it.
\end{abstract}
